Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

X1.name: Smart vs Premium vs Health Positioning Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to three product concepts (smart/subscription, premium/design, health). Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale. Randomization ensures each concept is shown to a random subset of participants.
X1.sample: 300 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three concepts (100 per concept). Recruitment targets individuals who have purchased a cooking appliance in the past 12 months.
X1.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent score for each concept.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Smart/subscription concept will have the highest average WTP and purchase intent, indicating demand for smart features and subscription services.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium/design concept will have the highest average WTP and purchase intent, indicating demand for status signaling and brand prestige.
prediction_by_theory.T3: Health concept will have the highest average WTP and purchase intent, indicating demand for a health-focused, low-impact cooking solution.

X1.decision_rule: If the smart/subscription concept's average WTP exceeds the premium/design concept by at least 1.5 points and is significantly higher than the health concept, proceed with a differentiated smart/subscription home‑cook proposition. If premium/design exceeds health by at least 1.5 points and is significantly higher than smart, proceed with a premium/design proposition. If health exceeds smart by at least 1.5 points and is significantly higher than premium, proceed with a health‑focused proposition. If none of the concepts meet the threshold, do not expand into home‑cook.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a full home‑cook expansion yet. The evidence base is weak: RATIONAL's customer base is commercial and professional, and its financial performance shows strong B2B margins but no home‑cook demand data. The smart‑subscription concept is the only one with plausible demand mechanism, but it is untested. A limited pilot (e.g., a subscription‑enabled model) would be the safest next step before scaling.
final.target_customer: Home cooks who value convenience, personalized cooking, and are willing to pay for smart features and recurring services.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated combi‑steamer that integrates smart technology, subscription services, and recipe learning, offering a time‑saving, personalized cooking experience.
final.next_action: Run a limited pilot of a subscription‑enabled combi‑steamer model with 100 home cooks, measuring willingness to pay and repeat purchase rates. Use the results to decide whether to scale the smart‑subscription proposition.
final.uncertainty: The demand for smart features and subscription services among home cooks is untested. Financial performance metrics do not address home‑cook demand, and the market potential is based on company estimates, not observable data.
would_change_if: A pilot shows low willingness to pay or low repeat purchase rates for the smart‑subscription concept.
Evidence emerges that premium positioning or health messaging drives higher purchase intent than smart features.
A competitor launches a successful subscription‑enabled combi‑steamer, indicating a viable market path.

arguments.name: Smart vs Premium vs Health Positioning Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to three product concepts (smart/subscription, premium/design, health). Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale. Randomization ensures each concept is shown to a random subset of participants.
arguments.sample: 300 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three concepts (100 per concept). Recruitment targets individuals who have purchased a cooking appliance in the past 12 months.
arguments.measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent score for each concept.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Smart/subscription concept will have the highest average WTP and purchase intent, indicating demand for smart features and subscription services.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium/design concept will have the highest average WTP and purchase intent, indicating demand for status signaling and brand prestige.
prediction_by_theory.T3: Health concept will have the highest average WTP and purchase intent, indicating demand for a health-focused, low-impact cooking solution.

arguments.decision_rule: If the smart/subscription concept's average WTP exceeds the premium/design concept by at least 1.5 points and is significantly higher than the health concept, proceed with a differentiated smart/subscription home‑cook proposition. If premium/design exceeds health by at least 1.5 points and is significantly higher than smart, proceed with a premium/design proposition. If health exceeds smart by at least 1.5 points and is significantly higher than premium, proceed with a health‑focused proposition. If none of the concepts meet the threshold, do not expand into home‑cook.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a description of a subscription-based combi-steamer that automates cooking and delivers recipes, with a monthly fee of €9.99. Group B receives a description of a premium-priced combi-steamer that emphasizes precision cooking and professional-grade results, with a price of €1,299. Both groups are shown a neutral product description to control for brand awareness. Participants are asked to indicate their likelihood to purchase (1-7) and the maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and cooking frequency.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 1-7 scale and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.who_benefits: Health-conscious home cooks willing to pay a premium for convenience and health advantages.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If RATIONAL frames the product as a modern, stylish appliance that delivers faster, healthier meals, they will shift from generic appliances to a premium offering.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Higher price points and repeat purchases from a niche segment of affluent home cooks.
assumptions: Home cooks perceive steam-cooking as a benefit.
There is a segment willing to pay a premium for design and convenience.
Marketing can differentiate RATIONAL's technology from competitors.
predictions: A survey of home cooks would show at least 30% would consider purchasing a premium combi-steamer at a price 20% above standard models.
Sales would be concentrated among demographics with higher disposable income and interest in culinary gadgets.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: If RATIONAL offers a compact, single-appliance solution that cooks multiple dishes simultaneously, home cooks will switch from a collection of separate appliances to a streamlined system.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Higher volume sales through a single product and repeat purchases due to convenience.
assumptions: Home cooks have limited cooking time and prefer one appliance for multiple tasks.
Time savings are a primary purchase driver for home cooks.
RATIONAL can demonstrate measurable time savings in product testing.
predictions: A pilot test of a compact combi-steamer would show at least 40% of participants reducing cooking time by at least 30 minutes per meal.
Purchase intent would be higher among households with children or multiple meals to prepare daily.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and a simulated purchase decision.
X1.sample: 500 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and household income.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and willingness to pay (WTP) for a premium vs. convenience-combi-steamer.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of respondents will express purchase intent for the premium-combi-steamer at a price 20% above standard models.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of respondents will express purchase intent for the convenience-combi-steamer, with WTP significantly higher than the premium version.

X1.decision_rule: If premium-combi-steamer intent >=30% AND premium WTP >= premium-combi-steamer WTP, recommend developing a differentiated premium proposition. X1.name: Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of 500 home cooks (aged 25-55) who have purchased a kitchen appliance in the past year. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription-based smart combi-steamer description emphasizing convenience, recurring revenue, and smart home integration; Group B sees a premium, high-performance combi-steamer description emphasizing professional-grade cooking, superior results, and brand prestige. Both groups view a neutral product description and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay a monthly subscription fee (or a premium price).
X1.sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (7-point scale) and willingness to pay (monthly subscription fee or premium price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a subscription fee than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium price than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in average purchase intent between Group A and Group B is at least 1.5 points (e.g., Group A = 5.5 and Group B = 4.0), we conclude that the subscription messaging (T1) is more effective. If the difference is at least 1.5 points in favor of the premium messaging (Group B = 5.5 and Group A = 4.0), we conclude that premium positioning (T2) is more effective. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, we conclude neither theory is significantly supported and recommend further market research.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed subscription vs premium messaging test (X1) to empirically compare home cook demand for a subscription-based smart combi-steamer versus a premium, high-performance model. If the test shows a ≥1.5-point difference in purchase intent in favor of subscription messaging, develop a differentiated subscription proposition; otherwise, maintain the premium positioning and consider additional market research.
final.target_customer: Home cooks who value convenience, recurring revenue, and smart home integration, as identified by the test.
final.value_proposition: A subscription-based smart combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, leveraging RATIONAL's existing B2B reputation to build trust.
final.next_action: Execute the 12-week, €8,000 online survey test with 500 home cooks, randomized to subscription or premium messaging, and analyze results against the 1.5-point decision threshold.
final.uncertainty: The test results are pending; without actual data, the strength of demand for a subscription model is unknown. Additionally, the premium positioning's effectiveness is also uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows a ≥1.5-point difference in favor of premium messaging, we would shift to premium positioning and reconsider subscription.
If the test shows no significant difference or a difference <1.5 points, we would recommend further market research before committing to either strategy.

position.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated home-cook proposition yet. frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

X1.name: Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from home cooks who have purchased a kitchen appliance in the past 12 months. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription-based combi-steamer description emphasizing automation, recurring recipe updates, and monthly fees; Group B sees a premium-combi-steamer description emphasizing professional-grade performance, durability, and high-quality cooking results. Both groups view product images and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and willingness to pay a premium price (EUR 1,000).
X1.sample: 400 home cooks (200 per group), recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay premium (EUR 1,000).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group A.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 6.5), recommend pursuing the subscription-based differentiated proposition. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, recommend pursuing the premium positioning. If the difference is less than 5 points, indicate uncertainty and suggest further testing.

revisions.reason: The simulated warehouse test (SYN-D) concerns a label printer and packing errors, which does not address home-cook demand for subscription-based automation. Therefore it bears on no theory and changes nothing.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated home-cook proposition yet. The evidence shows RATIONAL already serves commercial kitchens and has no public data on home-cook demand, subscription willingness, or premium positioning. The subscription test (X1) is the next affordable step to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay before any product development.
final.target_customer: Home cooks who cook frequently and seek professional-level results, as indicated by the premium positioning theory.
final.value_proposition: A premium, high-performance combi-steamer that delivers consistent, professional-grade cooking results, positioned as a professional-grade appliance for serious home cooks.
final.next_action: Run the proposed subscription vs premium messaging test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay, and use the decision rule to decide whether to pursue the subscription-based or premium positioning.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on home-cook demand, willingness to pay recurring fees, and premium positioning effectiveness.
would_change_if: If the subscription test shows purchase intent at least 5 points higher than premium positioning, we would shift to recommend the subscription-based differentiated proposition.
If the premium test shows purchase intent at least 5 points higher than subscription positioning, we would shift to recommend the premium positioning.
If neither test meets the threshold, we would maintain uncertainty and suggest further testing.

arguments.name: Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from home cooks who have purchased a kitchen appliance in the past 12 months. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription-based combi-steamer description emphasizing automation, recurring recipe updates, and monthly fees; Group B sees a premium-combi-steamer description emphasizing professional-grade performance, durability, and high-quality cooking results. Both groups view product images and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and willingness to pay a premium price (EUR 1,000).
arguments.sample: 400 home cooks (200 per group), recruited via an online panel to ensure demographic diversity.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay premium (EUR 1,000).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score and higher willingness to pay a premium than Group A.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 6.5), recommend pursuing the subscription-based differentiated proposition. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, recommend pursuing the premium positioning. If the difference is less than 5 points, indicate uncertainty and suggest further testing.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated home-cook proposition yet. The evidence shows RATIONAL already serves commercial kitchens and has no public data on home-cook demand, subscription willingness, or premium positioning. The subscription test (X1) is the next affordable step to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay before any product development.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters, leveraging the growing demand for commercial-quality residential laundry solutions. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and renters who lack time or space for a full-size washer/dryer, and landlords/building managers seeking to attract tenants.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing urbanization and time constraints make laundry a service rather than a household chore; consumers prefer quick, self-service options over owning a machine.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value by selling compact, self-service machines at a premium price through retail channels, leveraging its professional reputation for reliability.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for convenience and reliability.
Retail distribution can reach target homeowners/renters.
Competitive landscape does not deter adoption of a differentiated consumer proposition.
predictions: In a test offering a compact self-service machine in a residential building, at least 30% of tenants will rent the machine within 3 months.
Willingness to pay will be at least 20% above the price of a standard professional model.

assumptions: Small businesses are willing to pay a premium for reliability and uptime.

Competitive offerings do not deter adoption of a differentiated consumer proposition.
predictions: In a test offering a compact machine to a group of small businesses, at least 25% will place an order within 6 months.

X1.name: Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offers and willingness-to-pay questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners/renters and 250 small businesses (gyms, marinas, campsites). Recruit via social media and industry forums.
X1.measure: 1) Share of respondents who express intent to rent/purchase the product. 2) Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros. 3) Intent to place an order within 6 months.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher intent and WTP than small businesses, with at least 30% of homeowners intending to rent/purchase and WTP at least 20% above a standard professional model.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small businesses will show higher intent and WTP than homeowners, with at least 25% of small businesses intending to place an order and WTP at least 15% above a standard professional model.

X1.decision_rule: If homeowners' intent and WTP exceed small businesses' by at least 10 percentage points and by at least 15% of the WTP threshold, proceed with a differentiated homeowner proposition. If small businesses' intent and WTP exceed homeowners' by at least 10 percentage points and by at least 15% of the WTP threshold, proceed with a differentiated small‑business proposition. If neither segment meets its threshold, do not expand.

revisions.reason: The simulated result SYN-EPRO-UPDATE does not address homeowner demand, willingness to pay, or the specific motivations of homeowners and renters, so it does not affect T1.

final.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test (500 respondents, €18,000, 8 weeks) to measure intent and willingness to pay. If homeowners meet the 10‑percentage‑point and 15‑percentage‑point thresholds, proceed to pilot; otherwise, do’
final.uncertainty: The size of the homeowner market, actual willingness to pay, and the competitive landscape for compact residential machines are uncertain. The test will resolve these uncertainties.
would_change_if: If the test shows small‑business intent and willingness to pay exceeding homeowners by at least 10 percentage points and 15% of the WTP threshold, shift focus to a small‑business proposition.
If no segment meets its threshold, abandon expansion and continue focusing on professional offerings.

result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

tool_result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters, leveraging the growing residential demand for commercial-quality home laundry solutions. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test willingness to pay and demand for compact self-service machines, using the proposed Consumer vs Business Messaging Test to validate the premium price point and convenience motivation before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

Electrolux can produce machines that meet consumer expectations for compact size and performance.
predictions: In a test market, consumers will choose a compact self-service machine over a standard professional model when price is comparable.
Sales of compact consumer machines will increase in regions with high homeownership rates.
Consumers will report higher satisfaction with reduced wait times compared to traditional laundry.

X1.name: Consumer vs Business Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offers and willingness-to-pay questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 homeowners/renters and 250 small business operators (hotels, gyms, campsites). Recruit via targeted social media and industry forums.
X1.measure: 1) Willingness to pay a premium over a standard professional model (price difference). 2) Intent to purchase (binary: would buy). 3) Primary motivation (convenience vs cost savings).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher willingness to pay for a compact self-service machine than small businesses, and will cite convenience as the primary motivation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small businesses will show higher willingness to pay for a compact self-service machine than homeowners, and will cite cost savings as the primary motivation.

X1.decision_rule: If homeowners' willingness to pay exceeds small businesses' willingness to pay by at least 10% and convenience is the top stated motivation, proceed to develop a differentiated home proposition. If small businesses' willingness to pay exceeds homeowners' by at least 10% and cost savings is the top stated motivation, develop a differentiated small‑business proposition. If neither segment's willingness to pay exceeds the other by 10% or both motivations are equally strong, do not expand.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) does not address homeowners' willingness to pay for self-service solutions or their preference for compact machines over traditional models. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners and renters, leveraging the growing residential demand for commercial-quality home laundry solutions. Begin with a small-scale pilot to test willingness to pay and demand for compact self-service machines, using the proposed Consumer vs Business Messaging Test to validate the premium price point and convenience motivation before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and renters in urban and suburban areas who lack time or space for a traditional laundry room.
final.value_proposition: Compact, consumer-focused self-service machines that deliver professional-grade washing and drying performance, reducing wait times and effort while offering a premium price for convenience and reliability.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer vs Business Messaging Test (500 respondents, €18,000, 10 weeks) to measure willingness to pay and primary motivation before committing to a full product launch.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company assertions and one simulated result; no real consumer demand data exists. The test will resolve whether homeowners are willing to pay a premium for self-service solutions.
would_change_if: If the test shows homeowners' willingness to pay for a compact machine is at least 10% lower than small businesses' willingness to pay, or if cost savings are the primary motivation, we would shift focus to a small‑business proposition.
If additional independent data shows strong consumer demand for home laundry solutions, we would reconsider the consumer proposition.
If the simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) were confirmed, we would revise T1 and explore a different route to market.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.

X1.name: Segmented Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) space‑constrained home segment (emphasizing compact design and convenience), (2) small business/gym segment (emphasizing reliability, low maintenance, and high volume), (3) neutral control. Each group sees a product description of a consumer‑grade machine (Electrolux Generation 7000) with a price point. The test measures purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 1‑5 scale.
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and housing type (homeowners vs renters). 150 per segment.
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants indicating "Would buy") and average WTP (mean of 1‑5 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Space‑constrained group will have the highest purchase intent and WTP, indicating demand for compact consumer machines.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small business/gym group will have the highest purchase intent and WTP, indicating demand for durable consumer machines.

X1.decision_rule: If the space‑constrained group exceeds the small business/gym group by at least 10 percentage points and its WTP is at least 1.5 points higher, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners/renters. If the small business/gym group exceeds the space‑constrained group by at least 10 percentage points and its WTP is at least 1.5 points higher, develop a proposition targeting small businesses/gyms. If neither segment exceeds the other by the 10‑point threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) does not address T1, as it tests the effect of durability-and-repairability messaging on purchase reservations, not homeowner demand for compact consumer machines. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Run the proposed Segmented Messaging Test to empirically compare demand for space‑constrained home versus small‑business/gym propositions. Until the test yields a clear 10‑point difference in purchase intent and willingness to pay, maintain focus on professional segments.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and renters with limited laundry space and those seeking hands‑on control of their laundry.
final.value_proposition: Compact, consumer‑grade machines sold through retail channels, leveraging Electron’x Professional brand to justify premium pricing while staying below consumer appliance market share.
final.next_action: Execute the 8‑week, €18,000 online survey test with randomized messaging exposure, measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay.
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand, price sensitivity, and market size. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the space‑constrained group exceeds the small‑business/gym group by at least 10 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 1.5 points higher, develop a differentiated home proposition.

If the small‑business/gym group exceeds the space‑constrained group by at least 10 percentage points and its willingness to pay is at least 1.5 points higher, develop a differentiated small‑business/gym proposition.

arguments.name: Segmented Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) space‑constrained home segment (emphasizing compact design and convenience), (2) small business/gym segment (emphasizing reliability, low maintenance, and high volume), (3) neutral control. Each group sees a product description of a consumer‑grade machine (Electrolux Generation 7000) with a price point. The test measures purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 1‑5 scale.
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, stratified by age and housing type (homeowners vs renters). 150 per segment.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants indicating "Would buy") and average WTP (mean of 1‑5 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Space‑constrained group will have the highest purchase intent and WTP, indicating demand for compact consumer machines.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small business/gym group will have the highest purchase intent and WTP, indicating demand for durable consumer machines.

arguments.decision_rule: If the space‑constrained group exceeds the small business/gym group by at least 10 percentage points and its WTP is at least 1.5 points higher, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners/renters. If the small business/gym group exceeds the space‑constrained group by at least 10 percentage points and its WTP is at least 1.5 points higher, develop a proposition targeting small businesses/gyms. If neither segment exceeds the other by the 10‑point threshold, do not expand into consumer markets.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Conduct the proposed Segmented Messaging Test to empirically compare demand for space‑constrained home versus small‑business/gym propositions. Until the test yields a clear 10‑point difference in purchase intent and willingness to pay, do not commit to a differentiated consumer proposition. result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

assumptions: Consumers value convenience and are willing to pay a premium for self-service.

X1.name: Self-service vs cost savings choice test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase choice. Participants view a product description of a self-service laundry unit and a comparable traditional machine. They are asked to indicate which they would choose and the maximum price they would pay. The survey also includes a brief demographic question about time availability and cost sensitivity.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for time availability (busy vs less busy) and cost sensitivity (high vs low).
X1.measure: Percentage of participants choosing the self-service unit and the average maximum price paid for the self-service unit.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 40% of participants will choose the self-service unit, and the average maximum price will be at least 20% higher than the traditional machine.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 40% of participants will choose the traditional machine, and the average maximum price will be at least 15% lower than the self-service unit.

X1.decision_rule: If the self-service unit is chosen by at least 40% of participants and its average maximum price is at least 20% higher than the traditional machine, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for convenience. If the traditional machine is chosen by at least 40% and its average maximum price is at least 15% lower, proceed to develop a cost‑saving proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer markets.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) does not provide real evidence of consumer preference for convenience versus cost savings; it is a hypothetical test of description effect. Therefore it does not affect the validity of T1.

result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners and renters are willing to pay for reliable, compact self-service laundry solutions that fit small spaces and reduce replacement frequency, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners and renters seeking convenient, cost-effective laundry options in limited spaces.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing demand for commercial‑quality products for residential use, coupled with obsolescence concerns about appliance lifespan, motivates consumers to choose durable, reliable solutions.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering premium‑priced, high‑performance self‑service machines sold directly to consumers or through retail/wholesale channels, leveraging its professional‑grade reputation.
assumptions: Consumer willingness to pay for professional‑grade reliability outweighs price sensitivity.
Limited space in residential units makes compact, space‑efficient designs attractive.
Electrolux can reach consumers through existing retail/wholesale channels without major infrastructure changes.
predictions: A test offering a compact self‑service unit in a residential building would achieve at least 10% trial adoption rate within 12 weeks.
Surveyed consumers would indicate intent to purchase at a price 20% above comparable consumer laundry units, but would still purchase if reliability is guaranteed.
Sales data from retail/wholesale channels would show a 15% increase in self‑service unit sales compared to baseline performance.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Operational efficiency and cost savings drive small businesses to seek durable, reliable equipment that minimizes downtime and replacement costs.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value by offering premium‑priced, high‑performance self‑service units sold through wholesale channels, leveraging its professional‑grade reputation to attract B2B customers.
assumptions: Small businesses prioritize reliability and efficiency over price.
Gyms and fitness centers have consistent, high‑volume laundry demand that can be met with self‑service solutions.
Electrolux can reach small businesses through existing wholesale networks without major infrastructure changes.
predictions: A pilot offering a compact self‑service unit to a group of small gyms would achieve at least 15% adoption rate within 12 weeks.
Surveyed small business owners would indicate intent to purchase at a price 15% above comparable consumer units, but would still purchase if reliability is guaranteed.
Wholesale sales data would show a 20% increase in self‑service unit sales compared to baseline performance.

X1.name: Segmented Pilot Test: Home vs Small Business
X1.method: Run a 12‑week pilot in two distinct locations: a residential building (homeowners/renters) and a group of small gyms. In each location, offer a compact self‑service unit at a price 15% above comparable consumer units. Track trial adoption (units installed or checked out) and purchase intent via a short survey. Collect data on reasons for adoption (space, reliability, cost).
X1.sample: Residential building: 50 units (approx. 100 trial users). Gyms: 10 units (approx. 20 trial users). Total 60 units.
X1.measure: Trial adoption rate (units installed/checked out) and purchase intent (percentage of trial users indicating intent to purchase at the premium price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Residential trial adoption ≥ 10% and gym trial adoption ≥ 10% with purchase intent ≥ 15% in both segments.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Gym trial adoption ≥ 15% and residential trial adoption ≥ 10% with purchase intent ≥ 15% in both segments.

X1.decision_rule: If both segments meet their respective adoption thresholds (residential ≥ 10% and gym ≥ 10%), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If only one segment meets its threshold, focus on that segment. If neither meets its threshold, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) does not address residential demand; it tests a description's incremental effect on purchase reservations, not actual consumer behavior. Therefore it does not affect T1, which predicts homeowner demand for compact, reliable self-service solutions.

final.recommendation: Run a segmented pilot test (residential vs. small business) to validate demand before committing to a differentiated consumer proposition. The pilot should measure trial adoption and purchase intent at a premium price to assess willingness to pay for reliability and compact design. If both segments meet their respective adoption thresholds, proceed to develop a consumer proposition; otherwise, focus on the better
final.target_customer: Homeowners and renters seeking convenient, cost‑effective laundry solutions in limited spaces, and small businesses and gyms with consistent, high‑volume laundry demand.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that offers compact, professional‑grade self‑service laundry units, emphasizing reliability, space efficiency, and reduced replacement frequency, sold through existing retail/wholesale channels.
final.next_action: Execute the proposed 12‑week pilot test with 50 residential units and 10 gym units, tracking trial adoption and purchase intent. Use the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a consumer proposition or focus on the better
final.uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to limited public evidence on consumer willingness to pay, actual purchase behavior, and market size. The pilot will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows both segments meeting their adoption thresholds, the recommendation would shift to develop a consumer proposition.
If neither segment meets its threshold, the recommendation would remain to focus on the existing professional offering or explore other alternatives.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.
Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product.

Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium health benefits and taste) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. X1.sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium health and taste messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability and waste reduction messaging).
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each condition.

arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium health benefits and taste) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Premium Condition (premium health and taste messaging) or Sustainability Condition (sustainability and waste reduction messaging).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑2 to 7) for each condition.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test (300 Danish adults, 10‑week timeline, €18,000) to measure purchase intent under each condition.
arguments.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer willingness to pay a premium for premium health benefits versus sustainability motivations.
would_change_if: If the pilot test shows Premium Condition mean purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and Sustainability Condition mean < 5.5, we would shift to a premium‑focused proposition.
If the pilot test shows Sustainability Condition mean ≥ 5.5 and Premium Condition mean < 5.5, we would shift to a sustainability‑focused proposition.
If neither condition meets its threshold, we would maintain the current B2B focus and conduct further market research.

X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑to 7) and top reason for choosing the product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to premium messaging will have a higher average purchase intent score and sustainability will be the top reason for a smaller subset of participants.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for premium messaging is at least 1.5 points higher than for sustainability messaging (p < 0.05), conclude that premium positioning drives higher intent. If sustainability messaging yields a higher average score, conclude that sustainability drives higher intent. If the difference is within 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further testing is recommended.

result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

X1.name: Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium health and taste positioning) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income to ensure representativeness.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and top reason for choosing the product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to premium messaging will report higher purchase intent and will cite health and taste as the top reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to sustainability messaging will report higher purchase intent and will cite sustainability as the top reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for premium messaging is at least 5 points higher than for sustainability messaging (i.e., premium ≥ 5.5 and sustainability ≤ 5.0), proceed with a premium‑priced differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, consider a sustainability‑focused proposition. If the difference is ≤ 2 points, do not commit to either positioning and conduct further market research.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.

X1.name: Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium health benefits and taste) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income to ensure representativeness.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and top reason for choosing the product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to premium messaging will report higher purchase intent and will cite taste and purity as the top reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to sustainability messaging will report higher purchase intent and will cite sustainability as the top reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for premium messaging is at least 5 points higher than for sustainability messaging (i.e., premium ≥ 5.5 and sustainability ≤ 5.0), proceed with a premium‑priced differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, consider a sustainability‑focused proposition. If the difference is ≤ 2 points, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

arguments.name: Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging condition. Participants view a product description of a differentiated home water purifier (e.g., premium health benefits and taste) and a description emphasizing sustainability and plastic waste reduction. They are then asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers in Denmark, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income to ensure representativeness.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and top reason for choosing the product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to premium messaging will report higher purchase intent and will cite taste and purity as the top reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to sustainability messaging will report higher purchase intent and will cite sustainability as the top reason.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for premium messaging is at least 5 points higher than for sustainability messaging (i.e., premium ≥ 5.5 and sustainability ≤ 5.0), proceed with a premium‑priced differentiated proposition. If the difference is less than 2 points, consider a sustainability‑focused proposition. If the difference is ≤ 2 points, do not commit to either proposition and conduct further market research.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

Simonelli can effectively communicate status positioning to consumers.

X1.name: Status vs Convenience Choice Test
X1.method: Online choice experiment with simulated purchase decisions.
X1.sample: 300 adult participants recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income levels.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and stated reason for purchase (status vs convenience).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants who view the machine as a visible purchase will report higher purchase intent when income is linked to status than when income is randomly assigned.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants who emphasize convenience will report higher purchase intent than those who focus on status.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the status condition exceeds the average for the convenience condition by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, conclude that status drives purchase decisions. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, conclude that convenience drives purchase decisions. If the difference is not statistically significant, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

revisions.reason: The simulated evidence SYN-SIMO-UPDATE does not address whether home barista purchases are driven by status or convenience; it only tests a learning offer among enthusiasts. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.next_action: Execute the 12‑week, €20,000 choice experiment with 300 participants to measure purchase intent under status and convenience conditions.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to public sources; no internal company data is available. The test will determine whether status or convenience drives purchase decisions, but the results are not yet known.
would_change_if: If the test shows the convenience condition outperforms the status condition by at least 1.5 points, the recommendation would shift to emphasize convenience-driven marketing.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.who_benefits: Home barista consumers seeking a premium coffee experience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from generic coffee to a specialized machine that offers consistent quality, ease of use, and design, leading them to purchase multiple units.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli Group can capture value through premium pricing, brand positioning as a lifestyle brand, and potential cross-selling of accessories and subscription services.
assumptions: Home barista market is growing despite economic uncertainty.
Consumers are willing to invest in high-quality coffee equipment.
Simonelli can effectively communicate the lifestyle value of its products.
predictions: Surveyed home barista consumers will indicate intent to purchase a premium espresso machine.
Sales of a differentiated consumer product will be higher in regions with higher disposable income.
Customers will express willingness to pay a price premium compared to standard consumer machines.

T2.claim: Simonelli Group will not develop a differentiated consumer proposition because the home barista market is small and unprofitable, and the company prioritizes its professional and commercial segments.
T2.who_benefits: Simonelli Group's existing professional and commercial customers, who benefit from the company's established brand and market presence.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The company lacks the resources and motivation to invest in a new consumer product when the market size is limited and the potential return is uncertain.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
