tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Lifestyle vs. Convenience
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Lifestyle Condition (premium design, social-sharing features) or Convenience Condition (compact, easy-to-use machine). Both conditions present the same Simonelli consumer product concept at a fixed price point. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across Lifestyle and Convenience conditions to test both hypotheses.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for the differentiated Simonelli consumer product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price in the Lifestyle Condition compared to the Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price in the Convenience Condition compared to the Lifestyle Condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the Lifestyle Condition is at least 5 points higher than in the Convenience Condition (i.e., Lifestyle ≥ Convenience + 5 points), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on lifestyle/social sharing. If the difference is less than 5 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and consider other alternatives.

revisions.reason: The simulated home-barista learning proposition test (SYN-SIMO-UPDATE) does not provide real evidence of consumer demand for lifestyle/social-sharing features; it is a hypothetical case-author construction. Therefore it does not affect the validity of T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes lifestyle and social sharing, as supported by the domestic market positioning of the Eagle One Prima and the importance of social interaction in coffee culture. Conduct the proposed Consumer Proposition Test to validate the hypothesis before committing to a full product launch.
final.target_customer: Individual consumers who view coffee equipment as a lifestyle and social identity, particularly those who frequently share their coffee experiences on social media.
final.value_proposition: A premium, design-forward Simonelli machine positioned as a status symbol and social-sharing tool, offering a differentiated experience that goes beyond functional performance.
final.next_action: Run the Consumer Proposition Test (400 participants, two conditions, purchase intent and price willingness) to measure whether lifestyle/social-sharing features drive higher demand than convenience features.
final.uncertainty: The test will determine whether consumers prioritize lifestyle/social-sharing features over convenience. If the difference is less than 5 points, the investment case weakens; if it exceeds 5 points, the recommendation remains strong.
would_change_if: If the test shows the Convenience Condition outperforms the Lifestyle Condition by at least 5 points, the recommendation would shift to a convenience-focused proposition.
If new evidence shows a significant decline in consumer demand for coffee equipment in 2023, the investment case would be reconsidered.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Lifestyle vs. Convenience
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Lifestyle Condition (premium design, social-sharing features) or Convenience Condition (compact, easy-to-use machine). Both conditions present the same Simonelli consumer product concept at a fixed price point. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 400 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced across Lifestyle and Convenience conditions to test both hypotheses.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for the differentiated Simonelli consumer product.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price in the Lifestyle Condition compared to the Convenience Condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price in the Convenience Condition compared to the Lifestyle Condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent in the Lifestyle Condition is at least 5 points higher than in the Convenience Condition (i.e., Lifestyle ≥ Convenience + 5 points), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on lifestyle/social sharing. If the difference is less than 5 points, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and consider other alternatives.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes lifestyle and social sharing, as supported by the domestic market positioning of the Eagle One Prima and the importance of social interaction in coffee culture. Conduct the proposed Consumer Proposition Test to validate the hypothesis before committing to a full product launch.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated home-barista learning proposition test (SYN-SIMO-UPDATE) does not provide real evidence of consumer demand for lifestyle/social-sharing features; it is a hypothetical case-author construction. Therefore it does not affect the validity of T1.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes lifestyle and social sharing, as supported by the domestic market positioning of the Eagle One Prima and the importance of social interaction in coffee culture. Conduct the proposed Consumer Proposition Test to validate the hypothesis before committing to a full product launch.
arguments.target_customer: Individual consumers who view coffee equipment as a lifestyle and social identity, particularly those who frequently share their coffee experiences on social media.
arguments.value_proposition: A premium, design-forward Simonelli machine positioned as a status symbol and social-sharing tool, offering a differentiated experience that goes beyond functional performance.
arguments.next_action: Run the Consumer Proposition Test (400 participants, two conditions, purchase intent and price willingness) to measure whether lifestyle/social-sharing features drive higher demand than convenience features.
arguments.uncertainty: The test will determine whether consumers prioritize lifestyle/social-sharing features over convenience. If the difference is less than 5 points, the investment case weakens; if it exceeds 5 points, the recommendation remains strong.
would_change_if: If the test shows the Convenience Condition outperforms the Lifestyle Condition by at least 5 points, the recommendation would shift to a convenience-focused proposition.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

X1.name: Home Barista Preference Survey
X1.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home barista demographics (self-identified coffee enthusiasts). They view two machine concepts: (A) a premium professional‑grade machine with advanced controls and a compact design, and (B) a convenience‑focused machine with simplified controls and a compact design. Participants rank the two machines on a 7‑point scale (1‑very important, 7‑not important) and indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. The survey also includes a brief demographic question to ensure representation.
X1.sample: 300 participants, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions to reflect home barista demographics. Recruitment through coffee forums, social media, and partner channels.
X1.measure: Primary measure: average ranking of the premium machine (T1) versus the convenience machine (T2) across participants. Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) for the premium machine.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants will rank the premium machine higher than the convenience machine and report higher willingness to pay for the premium machine.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants will rank the convenience machine higher than the premium machine and report higher willingness to pay for the convenience machine.

X1.decision_rule: If the average ranking of the premium machine is at least 1.5 points higher than the convenience machine and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for the premium professional use case. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and focus on the existing professional line.

arguments.name: Home Barista Preference Survey
arguments.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home barista demographics (self-identified coffee enthusiasts). They view two machine concepts: (A) a premium professional‑grade machine with advanced controls and a compact design, and (B) a convenience‑focused machine with simplified controls and a compact design. Participants rank the two machines on a 7‑point scale (1‑very important, 7‑not important) and indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) in euros. The survey also includes a brief demographic question to ensure representation.
arguments.sample: 300 participants, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions to reflect home barista demographics. Recruitment through coffee forums, social media, and partner channels.
arguments.measure: Primary measure: average ranking of the premium machine (T1) versus the convenience machine (T2) across participants. Secondary measure: average willingness to pay (WTP) for the premium machine.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants will rank the premium machine higher than the convenience machine and report higher willingness to pay for the premium machine.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants will rank the convenience machine higher than the premium machine and report higher willingness to pay for the convenience machine.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average ranking of the premium machine is at least 1.5 points higher than the convenience machine and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for the premium professional use case. If the difference is less than 1.5 points or not statistically significant, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition and focus on the existing professional line.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Smart home integration and subscription model reduce upfront cost and provide ongoing value, making the appliance attractive for occasional use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL captures value through subscription fees and premium pricing for smart features, while also leveraging its existing B2B reputation.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay recurring fees for smart cooking features.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks treat combi-steamers as a premium, high‑utility kitchen device; they would purchase one only if it is marketed as a lifestyle convenience that saves time and effort, and a maker that controls design and retail can charge a premium for that convenience.
T1.who_benefits: Individual home cooks who value convenience, health benefits, and the convenience of a single device.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If the device is positioned as a smart, one‑pot solution that requires less setup and cleaning, home cooks will switch from multiple traditional cookers to a single combi‑steamer, increasing per‑user purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Premium price point through brand control, limited‑edition designs, and subscription‑based accessories or software services that enhance the convenience proposition.
assumptions: Home cooks currently own multiple traditional cookers and find setup and cleaning cumbersome.
A premium price is acceptable if the device delivers measurable time‑saving and health benefits.
Marketing can effectively communicate the lifestyle convenience.
predictions: In a test offering a compact, smart combi‑steamer at a 20% premium over standard models, at least 30% of surveyed home cooks will state intent to purchase within six months.
Sales conversion will be higher among households with two or more existing cookers than among those with one cooker only.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks treat combi-steamers as a premium, high‑utility kitchen device; they would purchase one only if it is marketed as a lifestyle convenience that saves time and effort, and a maker that controls design and retail can charge a premium for that convenience.

T2.claim: Home cooks treat combi-steamers as a professional kitchen tool; they would purchase one only if it is marketed as a high‑performance, industrial‑grade device for commercial use, and a maker that controls design and distribution can command premium prices for durability and performance.
T2.who_benefits: Professional home cooks and small commercial chefs who need reliable, high‑volume cooking solutions.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If the device is positioned as a robust, industrial‑grade combi‑steamer designed for commercial kitchens, these users will choose it over consumer‑grade alternatives because they prioritize durability and performance.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Premium pricing justified by durability, industrial‑grade materials, and distribution through professional channels, with potential for volume sales in commercial settings.
assumptions: Professional home cooks currently use consumer‑grade cookers that fail under heavy use.
They are willing to pay a premium for a device that can handle high volumes and maintain performance.
Marketing can effectively communicate industrial‑grade quality and durability.
predictions: In a test offering a professional‑grade combi‑steamer at a 30% premium over standard models, at least 25% of surveyed professional home cooks will state intent to purchase within six months.
Sales conversion will be higher among households with existing commercial cookers than among those without.

X1.name: Home Cook vs Professional Cooker Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offers and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 respondents: 250 self-identified home cooks (households with two or more existing cookers) and 250 self-identified professional home cooks (households with existing commercial cookers). Recruit via panel to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) and WTP (maximum price they would pay). 2) Preference ranking: which product they would choose first. 3) Demographics: age, household income, and existing cooker ownership.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Home cooks will show higher purchase intent and WTP for the premium, lifestyle‑focused combi‑steamer than professional home cooks, and ranking will favor the lifestyle product.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professional home cooks will show higher purchase intent and WTP for the professional‑grade combi‑steamer than home cooks, and ranking will favor the professional product.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium lifestyle combi‑steamer achieves purchase intent ≥ 30% among home cooks and WTP ≥ €1,200, while the professional combi‑steamer achieves purchase intent ≥ 25% among professional home cooks and WTP ≥ €1,200, proceed with a differentiated home‑cook proposition. If neither threshold is met, stay with professional kitchens.

revisions.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home-cook demand for a premium lifestyle combi-steamer; it tests coordination friction, not appliance preference. Therefore it does not affect T1.

The technology can be adapted from commercial combi-steamer without major redesign costs.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will indicate higher intent to purchase a smart combi-steamer compared to a standard model.
Willingness to pay will be above the price point of a conventional combi-steamer.
Purchase intent will correlate with exposure to smart kitchen marketing.

X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=300). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a smart, connected combi-steamer description emphasizing convenience, recipe guidance, and modern technology; Group B sees a premium, durable combi-steamer description emphasizing professional-grade performance, long-term reliability, and a higher price point.
X1.sample: 300 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point Likert scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group B, because smart messaging aligns with home cooks' desire for convenience and technology.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group A, because premium messaging aligns with home cooks' desire for durability and long-term investment.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A average >= 5.5 and Group B average <= 4), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B's average is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is below 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.

revisions.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cook demand for a smart, connected combi-steamer; it tests only the impact of coordination friction on purchase decisions. Therefore it does not affect T1, which predicts home cooks will adopt a differentiated smart, connected model.

final.recommendation: Run the proposed Smart vs Premium Messaging Test (or a similar willingness-to-pay experiment) to empirically compare home cooks' purchase intent for a smart, connected combi-steamer versus a premium, durable model. If the smart messaging group shows a meaningful advantage, develop a differentiated home-cook proposition; if not, consider staying with professional kitchens or exploring other home-cooking opportunities.
final.target_customer: Home cooks who cook regularly and value convenience, modern technology, and time-saving solutions.
final.value_proposition: A smart, connected combi-steamer that offers recipe guidance, real-time monitoring, and seamless integration with smart kitchens, positioned as the future of home cooking.
final.next_action: Execute the 12‑week, €20,000 willingness-to-pay test with 300 home cooks, randomized by messaging, and analyze results against the 1.5‑point threshold.
final.uncertainty: Both theories remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on home cook willingness to pay for smart or premium features; the test is the primary source of resolution.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

X1.name: Convenience vs. Performance Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from home cooks who have used traditional cooking appliances. They are shown two identical combi-steamers (same features, price, and brand) with different descriptions: one emphasizing convenience and time-saving (e.g., 'Replace 5 appliances with one, save hours each week!'), and the other emphasizing gourmet performance and professional-quality results (e.g., 'Achieve even cooking and precise temperature control like a professional chef!'). Participants indicate purchase intent (1-7) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 300 home cooks (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the convenience-focused condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the performance-focused condition.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the convenience condition exceeds the performance condition by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 5.5 vs. 4.0), proceed with a premium-priced convenience proposition. If the performance condition exceeds by at least 1.5 points, proceed with a premium-priced performance proposition. If neither difference is significant, do not expand into either segment.

revisions.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home-cook demand or premium-pricing willingness, so it does not affect T1. The theory remains unchanged.

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers switch to combi-steamers when they perceive a device that can achieve professional-quality results, such as even cooking, precise temperature control, and reduced cooking time.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Rational AG captures value by selling premium-priced home units through its own brand, leveraging its reputation for professional-grade cooking and justifying higher margins.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to invest in a device that promises professional-quality cooking results.
The performance advantage of a combi-steamer is perceptible and can be communicated effectively to consumers.
Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that offers superior cooking outcomes.
predictions: In a test offering a high-performance home combi-steamer, purchase intent among home cooks will be higher than for a standard unit.
Willingness to pay will be significantly higher for the high-performance unit compared to a standard unit.

arguments.name: Convenience vs. Performance Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from home cooks who have used traditional cooking appliances. They are shown two identical combi-steamers (same features, price, and brand) with different descriptions: one emphasizing convenience and time-saving (e.g., 'Replace 5 appliances with one, save hours each week!'), and the other emphasizing gourmet performance and professional-quality results (e.g., 'Achieve even cooking and precise temperature control like a professional chef!'). Participants indicate purchase intent (1-7) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 300 home cooks (150 per condition) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1-7) and maximum price willingness to pay for each condition.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the convenience-focused condition.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the performance-focused condition.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the convenience condition exceeds the performance condition by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 5.5 vs. 4.0), proceed with a premium-priced convenience proposition. If the performance condition exceeds by at least 1.5 points, proceed with a premium-priced performance proposition. If neither difference is significant, do not expand into either segment.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home-cook demand or premium-pricing willingness, so it does not affect T1. The theory remains unchanged.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

X1.name: Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription‑based smart combi-steamer description emphasizing automation and recurring revenue; Group B sees a premium‑grade professional‑grade combi-steamer description emphasizing durability and performance. Both groups view product images and are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have a higher purchase intent score and a higher willingness to pay than Group B, indicating demand for automation and recurring revenue.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have a higher purchase intent score and a higher willingness to pay than Group A, indicating demand for premium, professional‑grade durability and performance.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 6.5), proceed with the subscription‑based smart combi-steamer development. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, proceed with the premium‑grade professional‑grade combi-steamer development. If the difference is less than 5 points, indicate uncertainty and recommend further market research.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.
